[TASK_TYPE=concept]
[BOUNDARY=crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
Why is a KEM with only CPA-style intuition not enough for an adversarial network protocol?

Because the network attacker is not limited to passive observation. They can inject malformed ciphertexts, trigger decryption behavior, and try to learn from protocol reactions. CPA-style security talks about secrecy under observation; CCA-style thinking is what protects active protocol use.

[TASK_TYPE=concept]
[BOUNDARY=crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
What practical lesson should an engineer take from the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform?

That turning a lattice-style encryption core into a robust KEM is not a cosmetic wrapper. FO-style reasoning is what closes the gap between a mathematically nice encryption primitive and a network-safe encapsulation mechanism under active attack.

[TASK_TYPE=security_analysis]
[BOUNDARY=crypto]
[SEVERITY=critical]
A developer says: "We already have a hard lattice problem under the hood, so malformed ciphertext handling is just an implementation detail." What should the reviewer conclude?

Reject that reasoning. Malformed ciphertext handling is part of the security story, not an afterthought. A hard underlying problem does not automatically give active-attack safety at the protocol boundary.

[TASK_TYPE=review]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=critical]
A Rust KEM wrapper returns different error variants and different response timing for parse failure, decapsulation failure, and authentication failure. Why is that dangerous?

Because it can turn protocol behavior into an oracle for active attackers. If failure modes are distinguishable through errors, timing, or downstream reactions, the wrapper may leak exactly the structure that CCA-oriented design is supposed to suppress.

[TASK_TYPE=implementation]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
When integrating a KEM into Rust transport code, what is the safe mindset about decapsulation results and fallback behavior?

Treat decapsulation failure as a security-critical path, not a convenience branch. Do not silently fall back to insecure defaults, alternate plaintext modes, or distinguishable protocol continuations. Failure handling must preserve the intended security envelope of the handshake.

[TASK_TYPE=attack_surface]
[BOUNDARY=crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
What kind of attack mindset does FO-style CCA reasoning train the engineer to expect?

An active attacker who crafts ciphertexts, observes reactions, and tries to learn from every difference in protocol handling. The point is not just that decryption should fail, but that failure should not become an information channel.

[TASK_TYPE=design]
[BOUNDARY=crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
Why is it often better to use a well-defined KEM construction than to improvise a custom public-key encryption + key-derivation handshake?

Because the hard part is not only deriving a shared secret, but doing so under active attack without accidental oracles or binding gaps. A standard KEM construction packages those lessons into the design, whereas custom encryption-plus-KDF flows often reintroduce exactly the problems the transform was invented to solve.

[TASK_TYPE=test_design]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
What should a minimal educational test suite include if it is meant to teach CCA-aware KEM integration discipline?

It should include at least: 1) successful encapsulate/decapsulate roundtrip; 2) malformed ciphertext rejection; 3) tests showing that different malformed inputs do not produce distinguishable high-level protocol behavior; 4) tests preventing insecure fallback on decapsulation failure.

[TASK_TYPE=explore]
[BOUNDARY=crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
Why is "it encrypts and decrypts fine in our demo" a weak argument for a KEM used in a real protocol?

Because demo success usually checks only the happy path. Real protocol security depends on how the system behaves under malformed ciphertexts, wrong keys, replayed messages, and active probing. FO-style thinking exists precisely because the happy path is not the whole threat model.

[TASK_TYPE=planning]
[BOUNDARY=rust+crypto]
[SEVERITY=major]
A team wants to add a lattice KEM to a Rust transport layer. What should be checked before they claim the handshake is "done"?

They should check more than successful key agreement: malformed ciphertext handling, failure uniformity, framing and serialization boundaries, transcript/domain binding, replay considerations, and the absence of insecure fallback behavior. A handshake is not done when roundtrip works; it is done when the active-attack surface is understood and controlled.
